name: Aragonese
family: Indo-European, Romance, Western Romance (Pyrenean, between Ibero-Romance and Occitano-Romance)
variety: Common written Aragonese read with a central and western Pyrenean pronunciation; segmental detail from the Chistabino illustration (Mott 2007)
sources: Mott, Brian (2007). Chistabino (Pyrenean Aragonese). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 37(1), 103-114.
Nagore Laín, Francho (1989). Gramática de la lengua aragonesa. 5th edition. Zaragoza: Mira Editores.
Mott, Brian (1989). El habla de Gistaín. Huesca: Instituto de Estudios Altoaragoneses.
Zamora Vicente, Alonso (1967). Dialectología española. 2nd edition. Madrid: Gredos.
contrasts: five vowels /i e a o u/ in stressed and unstressed syllables, without length or nasal contrasts (eastern Ribagorzan varieties add open-mid vowels)
three voiceless fricatives at front places, /θ/, /s/ and /ʃ/ (written z or c, s, x), and the affricate /tʃ/ (ch)
/l/ versus /ʎ/ and /n/ versus /ɲ/; /ʎ/ is frequent (muller, fillo, viello, güello)
voiced and voiceless stops; central Pyrenean varieties keep Latin voiceless stops between vowels (capeza, lupo) and voice stops after nasals and liquids
/x/ occurs only in loans from Castilian
allophony: /b d ɡ/ are approximants [β ð ɣ] except after a pause or a nasal (and /d/ after /l/), as in Spanish
word-final r is silent in most varieties: cantar [kanˈta], muller [muˈʎe]; the plural -rs is [s]; western valleys pronounce it
word-final t is silent in most varieties, above all after n (chent [tʃen], fuent [fwen], mont [mon]); final -at, -ut of nouns is [a], [u] or keeps a weak [t] by area
/s/ is apico-alveolar, as in northern Peninsular Spanish
/ʃ/ is often preceded by a glide [j] after a vowel (baixo, caixa), which some spellings write
nasals assimilate in place to a following consonant; word-final n is alveolar
unstressed vowels keep their quality; final unstressed e and o are often lost historically (chen, nueit), which creates final consonants and clusters
diphthongs ue, ie appear also before palatals (fuella, güello, viello) and vary by valley with ua, ia
phonotactics: initial clusters pl, cl, fl are kept (plorar, clamar, flama) and initial f is kept (fillo, fabla, fuella)
word-final consonants and clusters are more frequent than in Spanish because of vowel loss (nt, rt, ls, ns, z)
stress on the antepenultimate syllable is avoided in traditional speech, which moves it to the penultimate (medico, pachina)

stress.type: lexical, on one of the last two syllables in traditional speech
stress.rule: Words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the penultimate syllable and other words on the last, as in Spanish spelling; exceptions carry a written accent.
stress.cues: duration, pitch and intensity; no vowel reduction

rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for Aragonese are cited here; the classification follows the neighbouring Romance languages without vowel reduction.

length.notes: No length contrast; the trill versus tap contrast is the only one that involves duration.

intonation.declarative: rising accents on stressed syllables before the nucleus and a fall to low on the last stressed syllable
intonation.yes_no_question: final rise after the last stressed syllable, without change of word order
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then a fall to a low ending
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise through the stressed syllable with the peak at its end or in the next syllable
intonation.notes: Aragonese intonation is poorly documented. The entries give the general northern Ibero-Romance pattern and should be read as low confidence.

problems: written x is read [ks] between vowels unless an i precedes (caxa [kˈaksa], baxo [bˈakso]); in Aragonese spelling x stands for /ʃ/ (only initial x, x after i or after a consonant, and the digraphs aix, uix give [ʃ])
word-final r is always pronounced (muller [muʎˈeɾ], cantar [kantˈaɾ]), although it is silent in most varieties; only the plural -rs is reduced
open-mid [ɛ ɔ] are used in diphthongs and some other positions (pueyo [pwˈɛjɔ], fuella [fwˈɛʎa], ye [jˈɛ]); Aragonese has plain mid [e o]
muito is stressed on the i ([muˈito]) instead of having the diphthong [ˈmujto]
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used rather than the Spanish set
the rules and the exception list are small (290 and 528 lines), so many words fall back on Spanish-like defaults
good: /ʎ/, /tʃ/, /θ/ and /ɲ/ are present, and /ʃ/ is produced in ixo, ixe and word-initially
approximant [β ð ɣ] after vowels, inherited from the Spanish table
final t after a stressed vowel is a silent phoneme (shown as tʰ in the IPA output), which fits the varieties with mute final t (chent, ciudat, verdat)
initial f, pl, cl, fl and the diphthongs ue, ie are read as written

notes: Aragonese has several competing orthographies; the rules follow a spelling with ch, x, z and final -t, -r written. The phoneme table inherits Spanish and adds four phonemes.
